claim: Su Shi's official biography: the 1057 exam and Ouyang Xiu's assessment, provincial postings, opposition to the New Policies, the Crow Terrace case and Huangzhou exile, the Hangzhou governorship and West Lake/causeway works, the Huizhou and Hainan exiles, death in 1101, and posthumous honors.
author_or_org: Toqto'a (Tuotuo) and the Yuan-dynasty Song History compilers
source_title: History of Song (Song Shi), juan 338, Su Shi biography
limitations: Read via a Chinese Wikisource transcription, summarized by an automated fetch tool rather than line by line; most internal dates are reign-year era names, converted using standard era tables; one direct quotation (Ouyang Xiu's line) verified verbatim.

claim: A reflection, two years into the Huangzhou exile, that nothing not truly owned is worth taking, while the river breeze and mountain moon are nature's unenclosed, inexhaustible share.
source_title: First Rhapsody on the Red Cliff (Qian Chibi Fu)
limitations: Partial read: opening line and the 'not truly mine' passage verified verbatim via the fetch tool; remainder of the text was described, not reproduced verbatim, this session. Edition: Guwen Guanzhi (Finest Ancient Prose) vol. 11.

claim: The second Red Cliff outing that winter: the solitary crane, and the dream of a Taoist.
source_title: Second Rhapsody on the Red Cliff (Hou Chibi Fu)
limitations: Full text (all three paragraphs) read via Wikisource, Guwen Guanzhi (Finest Ancient Prose) vol. 11 edition. The page itself flags an unresolved manuscript dispute over whether the text reads one Taoist or two, noted but not resolved here.

claim: Equanimity toward both the storm and the clear sky, caught in rain on the road to Shahu near Huangzhou.
source_title: Calming the Waves (Dingfengbo): Don't Listen to the Rain Piercing the Woods and Striking the Leaves
limitations: Full short poem and preface read on a personal poetry-translation site, not Wikisource itself; wording consistent with two secondary descriptions of the same lines found in search results.

claim: Written drunk through the night of the 1076 Mid-Autumn Festival, explicitly also thinking of brother Su Zhe (courtesy name Ziyou).
source_title: Prelude to Water Melody (Shuidiao Getou): Mid-Autumn Festival of the Bingchen Year (When Did the Bright Moon First Appear?)
limitations: Partial read: preface and the dedication to Su Zhe verified verbatim; the body and famous closing couplet were described, not reproduced verbatim, by the fetch tool this session, so they are not quoted in the dossier.

claim: Written months before death; sums up a life's work as three places of exile rather than any court title held.
source_title: Self-Inscription on a Portrait at Jinshan (Zi ti Jinshan huaxiang)
source_family: self-inscription poem (poem inscribed on a painting)
limitations: Full short piece (4 lines) reproduced by a secondary aggregator, not a critical scholarly edition; not independently cross-checked against a print edition of the collected poems this session.

claim: Advice to a young relative preparing for the exams: no shortcut, years of steady study, and a multi-pass reading method ('eight-sided').
author_or_org: Su Shi (letter), discussed by Yang Zhijiu
source_title: Another Reply to Wang Xiang (You da Wang Xiang shu), quoted in an essay on the "eight-sided" reading method
source_family: letter, quoted in a secondary essay
limitations: The quoted passage is transmitted via a modern essay analyzing the letter, not read directly from the original Jingjin Dongpo Wenji Shilue (Dongpo's Collected Writings, Presented to the Throne, with Outline of Events; juan 46) compilation; the essay gives no date for the letter itself.

claim: Cross-check for birth/death dates, marriages, the Huangzhou/Huizhou/Hainan exile sequence, and a caveat that the 'Dongpo pork' origin story is unverified legend.
limitations: Tertiary, continuously-edited reference; used only to cross-check dates and sequence, not for any direct quotation used as [quoted] in the dossier or views.

claim: Dates the memorial known as "Memorial to Emperor Shenzong" to the fourth year of the Xining era (1071), opposing the green-sprouts loan policy.
source_title: article on Su Shi's 1071 memorials to Emperor Shenzong
limitations: Popular magazine article, not an academic critical edition; the memorial's own text was not independently read this session, only this secondary description of its date and argument.

claim: In the Yuanyou-era dispute over hired labor vs. the old corvee system, Su Shi argued against Sima Guang's abrupt reversal, recognizing merits on both sides.
source_title: article on the Yuanyou-era labor-service law dispute
limitations: Secondary synthesis of the dispute; not independently verified against Su Shi's own memorial text on this specific question this session.

claim: Account of the Crow Terrace Poetry Case: censors built a case from circulated poems; an anecdote about prison poems sent to a brother; a scholar's note about growing more cautious with words afterward.
source_title: essay on the Crow Terrace Poetry Case ("A Literary Inquisition Involving Crows")
limitations: An anecdote-driven essay, not a critical edition; the two prison poems to a brother (Sent to Ziyou from Prison) are discussed but their exact wording was not independently verified this session, so they are not quoted.

claim: Wrote a poem praising lychees while exiled at Huizhou (A Huizhou Quatrain / Eating Lychees), read as self-consolation and continued good humor despite banishment.
source_title: "Deep in the Cicadas' Song, the Lychees Are Red" (food-history column discussing the poem)
limitations: Popular press discussion; the poem's exact wording was not independently confirmed against a primary edition this session, so it is described but not quoted.

claim: At Danzhou (Hainan), taught local and visiting students at the Wine-Carrying Hall (Zaijiu Tang) and wrote classical commentaries; a later record credits this with starting Hainan's scholarly tradition.
source_title: feature on Su Shi's exile home and the Wine-Carrying Hall/Dongpo Academy on Hainan
limitations: Modern feature article; cites a Ming-dynasty source (Tang Zhou) for the 'Hainan scholars began from Danzhou' claim, which was not independently checked against that original text this session.
